title: Time and energy budgets in a migratory songbird: Daylength as a fundamental factor
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Migratory birds must balance their time and energy to successfully complete their journeys. Because migratory flights incur a high rate of energy consumption, but fuel deposition occurs at a much slower rate, migration should be dominated by the time and energy required for fuelling on the ground. Moreover, variation in daylength along the migratory route may further constrain fuelling time, affecting daily energy intake and turnover. Quantifying time and energy expenditure across the annual cycle is therefore essential for understanding the energetic and temporal constraints shaping migration strategies, yet these are intrinsically difficult to estimate in migratory birds. By integrating high-resolution migratory flight duration from multisensor biologging with thermoregulatory modelling and wind-tunnel measurements of flight energy expenditure, we reconstructed day-by-day time and energy budgets of thrush nightingales (Luscinia luscinia) across the full annual cycle. We quantified energy expenditure during migratory flight, thermoregulation and other locomotor activities, compared autumn and spring migration and tested how daily energy expenditure varied with daylength along the route. We provide the first quantitative estimate of total annual energy expenditure for a long-distance migratory songbird. Despite similar total flight duration in autumn and spring, both time and energy budgets differed between migratory seasons. In spring, non-flight activities consumed 2.1 times the energy spent on flight, and birds used 6.4 times more time on the ground than on migratory flights. In autumn, these ratios increased to 4.2 and 14, respectively. Importantly, longer days were associated with greater daily energy expenditure, indicating that longer photoperiods enable greater energy turnover, particularly in spring, when daily energy demands were the highest. Time and energy budgets during spring migration matched maximum energy deposition rates from optimal migration theory, whereas autumn migration involved more time and energy on the ground. We propose that season-specific daylength trends along the migratory routes, that is, lengthening in spring and declining in autumn, underlie the observed seasonal differences in migration patterns. Our findings provide quantitative annual time and energy budgets in a migratory passerine and identify daylength as a fundamental constraint shaping the seasonal migration patterns.
